name: Eye color diet

lead: The eye colour diet is the claim that eating or avoiding certain foods, or taking supplements and staying hydrated, can lighten or change your iris colour. It circulates in wellness and appearance communities as a route that needs no lenses or procedures.

Proponents generally suggest diet reduces iris melanin or brightens the eyes. Reference works describe iris colour as set mainly by melanin and genes such as OCA2 and HERC2 and do not list diet as an influence. Grokipedia states hydration does not change iris pigmentation, though it may improve the overall look of the eyes. No clinical study has tested a diet for eye colour.

paras: People adopt specific food lists, hydration habits or supplements and follow them over months, often alongside other eye-care habits.

No direct eye harms are reported for dietary approaches in the sources reviewed, though restrictive diets carry their own considerations. Sudden real colour change can signal a medical condition, and ophthalmology bodies warn against eye-colour-changing procedures and drops.

angle.text: Wellness and appearance forums promote foods, hydration and supplements as ways to lighten the iris without lenses or procedures. Reference works attribute iris colour to melanin and genes, and no trial has tested diet for eye colour.

lead: The eye color diet refers to claims that particular foods, supplements, hydration habits or eating patterns can lighten or otherwise change the color of the iris. It circulates in wellness content and appearance-focused online discussion as a way to get lighter, brighter eyes without colored lenses or procedures. Because eyes are among the first features people notice, the aim is a more striking or lighter eye color, and some versions of the idea also aim at whiter, clearer-looking eyes [1][2].

Reference works describe iris color as determined by the amount of melanin in the iris and by how light scatters in its stroma, with genes such as OCA2 and HERC2 the main known contributors [3]. In a 2014 Yahoo Health article, a raw-food blogger described her dark brown eyes turning hazel on a raw diet and linked the change to iridology; the article reported that eye doctors it quoted had not seen a study linking food to iris color, while one blogger's account of brighter-looking, less puffy eyes was treated as a different matter [1].

The American Academy of Ophthalmology has addressed a related folk practice, putting honey in the eyes to lighten them, and warns against placing foreign substances in the eye [2]. No published clinical study has tested a diet for changing iris color.
infobox: Lighten or change iris color; brighter-looking eyes

paras: Versions of the claim vary: some propose eliminating certain foods, others recommend particular vitamins, herbs, fruit-heavy or raw-food regimens, with the stated aim of reducing iris melanin or making the eyes appear lighter. The 2014 Yahoo Health article describes blogger Kristina Carrillo-Bucaram of FullyRaw, whose video about her eyes changing from dark brown to hazel drew about 1.3 million views, along with another raw-food chef who reported similar changes and a third who reported that her eyes looked brighter and less puffy [1].
Carrillo-Bucaram tied the change to iridology, a practice holding that iris patterns and colors reveal disease or "toxicity", and said her diet had cleansed her body and her eyes [1].

sections.h: What is known about eye color
paras: Iris color depends on melanin in the back and front layers of the iris and on how light scatters in the stroma; blue is a structural color with no blue pigment, and green combines a yellowish pigment with that scattering [3]. It is polygenic, with up to 16 genes implicated and HERC2 and OCA2 on chromosome 15 the main contributors [3].

A 1997 study of White Americans found that about 17 percent of children's eye color changed by adulthood, with equal numbers becoming lighter and darker; hazel and light brown eyes tended to lighten, and green eyes often darkened [3]. Some prostaglandin analogue medicines can increase pigmentation in one eye, and sudden changes in adults can accompany conditions such as cataract, glaucoma or iris atrophy [3].

Perceived eye brightness can vary with factors that do not alter the iris, such as sclera whiteness, redness, lighting and pupil size, and Grokipedia says hydration may improve the overall look of the eyes without changing iris pigmentation.

Dr. Deeba Chaudri of Cosmopolitan Eye Care told Yahoo Health that food does not affect iris pigment and that she had never seen a study linking food to eye color, though nutrition supports eye health. Dr. Juan Horta-Santini said neither a cornea nor a retina specialist he consulted had heard of diet changing eye color, and advised anyone who believes it did to see a specialist to rule out systemic disease [1].

The American Academy of Ophthalmology, answering a question about honey drops in 2013 (Omar R. Chaudhary, MD), called the idea "an urban myth", said the iris and not anything on the eye's surface determines color, and suggested colored contact lenses approved by an ophthalmologist as an alternative [2].
No studies found. No published human study has examined whether any diet or supplement changes iris color.

lore.intro: Claims of diet-linked eye color change spread mainly through raw-food and wellness bloggers and video comments, where they are often tied to detox ideas and iridology [1].

claims.claim: A raw-food diet changed eyes from dark brown to hazel.
Raw eating makes eyes look brighter and less puffy.
Honey applied to the eyes lightens them.

timeline.event: The American Academy of Ophthalmology answers a question about honey to lighten eyes [2].
